title: Electricity & Circuits
description: Current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's Law, series and parallel circuits, electrical power, and domestic electricity safety.

notes.heading: Current, Voltage and Charge
notes.body: Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of electric charge. I = Q/t (amperes, A). 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. In a metal wire, current is carried by free (delocalised) electrons moving from negative to positive. Conventional current flows from positive to negative (historical convention). Charge (Q) is measured in coulombs (C). One electron carries −1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. Voltage (potential difference, V) is the energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q (volts, V). 1 V = 1 J/C. The battery/power supply provides the 'push' (emf). Components convert electrical energy: resistors → heat, lamps → light + heat, motors → kinetic.

illustration.alt: Diagram of electron flow through a wire and a battery providing potential difference.
illustration.caption: Current is the rate of flow of charge; voltage is the energy per unit charge.

notes.heading: Resistance and Ohm's Law
notes.body: Resistance (R) opposes current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). Ohm's Law: V = IR (at constant temperature). An ohmic conductor has a constant resistance — its I-V graph is a straight line through origin. Non-ohmic conductors: filament lamp — resistance increases as it heats up (I-V graph curves). Diode — only conducts in one direction (very high resistance in reverse). Factors affecting resistance: length (R ∝ length — longer wire = more resistance), cross-sectional area (R ∝ 1/area — thicker wire = less resistance), material (resistivity — copper low, nichrome high), temperature (higher temperature = higher resistance in metals — ions vibrate more, more electron collisions).

illustration.alt: I-V characteristic graphs for an ohmic conductor, filament lamp, and diode.
illustration.caption: Ohmic conductors have constant resistance; the filament lamp and diode are non-ohmic.

notes.heading: Series Circuits
notes.body: Series: components connected in a single loop. Rules: (1) Current is the SAME everywhere: I₁=I₂=I₃. (2) Total voltage is SHARED: V_total=V₁+V₂+V₃. (3) Total resistance ADDS: R_total=R₁+R₂+R₃. Adding more resistors in series increases total resistance → current decreases. If one component breaks, the circuit is broken → all components stop working (old Christmas tree lights). Ammeters are always connected in SERIES (to measure current through a component).

illustration.alt: Series circuit diagram with ammeter, voltmeters, and the three rules for series circuits.
illustration.caption: In series, current is the same everywhere, voltages add, and resistances add.

notes.heading: Parallel Circuits
notes.body: Parallel: components connected on separate branches. Rules: (1) Total current SPLITS at junctions: I_total=I₁+I₂+I₃. (2) Voltage across each branch is the SAME as the source: V₁=V₂=V_total. (3) Total resistance DECREASES as more branches are added: 1/R_total=1/R₁+1/R₂+1/R₃. Adding a parallel branch provides an additional path → total resistance decreases → total current from battery increases. Each branch operates independently — if one breaks, others continue working. Domestic wiring is parallel: each appliance gets full mains voltage (~230 V in UK), can be switched independently, and a fault on one does not affect others. Voltmeters are connected in PARALLEL (to measure voltage across a component).

illustration.alt: Parallel circuit diagram with branch ammeters and the three rules for parallel circuits.
illustration.caption: In parallel, current splits, voltage is the same across branches, and total resistance decreases.

notes.heading: Electrical Power and Energy
notes.body: Power: P = VI (watts). Also P = I²R and P = V²/R (from Ohm's Law substitution). Energy transferred: E = Pt = VIt (joules). For domestic electricity, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3,600,000 J. Cost = power (kW) × time (h) × price per kWh. Example: 2000 W (2 kW) heater used for 3 hours → energy = 6 kWh. At £0.30/kWh → cost = £1.80. This is why high-power appliances (heaters, kettles, ovens) cost more to run even for short periods. Energy-saving bulbs (LED) provide same light output at much lower wattage → lower running costs.

illustration.alt: Power formulas P=VI, P=I²R, P=V²/R and a worked energy cost calculation in kilowatt-hours.
illustration.caption: Electrical power is measured in watts; domestic energy is billed in kilowatt-hours.

notes.heading: Domestic Electricity and Safety
notes.body: UK mains electricity: ~230 V AC, 50 Hz. Three wires in a plug: Live (brown) — carries alternating voltage. Neutral (blue) — completes the circuit, at ~0 V. Earth (green/yellow) — safety wire; connected to ground. If a fault causes the live wire to touch the metal case, current flows through earth wire to ground → large current → fuse blows or circuit breaker trips → disconnects. Fuse: thin wire that melts if current exceeds rated value (3A, 5A, 13A). Circuit breaker: electromagnetic switch that trips on overcurrent — reusable. Double insulation: appliances with plastic cases don't need earth wire. RCD (Residual Current Device): detects difference in live vs neutral current (leakage to earth/through a person) and cuts power in milliseconds. Safety rules: no wet hands, no damaged cables, proper fusing, don't overload sockets.

illustration.alt: UK three-pin plug wiring with live, neutral, and earth wires, plus fuse and circuit breaker safety features.
illustration.caption: The earth wire and fuse work together to prevent electric shock and fire.

notes.heading: Static Electricity (Electrostatics)
notes.body: Static electricity is the buildup of electric charge on insulating materials. Caused by friction transferring electrons between surfaces. Rubbing a plastic rod with cloth → rod gains electrons → negatively charged; cloth loses electrons → positively charged. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. This explains: hair standing up after removing a hat, dust sticking to TV screens, lightning (charge separation in clouds → discharge). Sparks occur when charge rapidly jumps across a gap (mini lightning). Dangers: sparks near flammable vapours (petrol stations), electrostatic discharge damaging electronics. Uses: photocopiers and laser printers (toner attracted to charged drum), electrostatic paint spraying (charged paint droplets attracted to earthed car body), precipitators (remove smoke particles from factory chimneys). Earthing: connecting an object to ground allows charge to flow away safely — fuel tankers have earthing straps.

illustration.alt: Charge transfer by friction between a plastic rod and cloth, showing the rod gaining electrons.
illustration.caption: Static electricity is the build-up of electric charge on insulating materials.

flashcards.definition: Rate of flow of charge: I=Q/t. Measured in amperes (A). 1 A = 1 C/s.
flashcards.example: 12 C pass in 4 s → I = 3 A.

flashcards.definition: Energy per unit charge: V=E/Q. The 'push' driving current. Measured in volts (V).
flashcards.example: Battery provides 1.5 V → 1.5 J per coulomb of charge.

flashcards.definition: Opposition to current: R=V/I. Measured in ohms (Ω).
flashcards.example: 3 V across component, 0.5 A current → R=6 Ω.

flashcards.definition: V=IR at constant temperature. Ohmic conductor: I-V graph is straight line through origin.
Single loop. Same current everywhere. Voltages add. Resistances add. One break = all off.
flashcards.example: Old Christmas lights — one bulb fails, all go out.

flashcards.definition: Multiple branches. Current splits. Voltage same across branches. Total resistance < smallest branch. Independent operation.
flashcards.example: Home wiring — each appliance gets 230 V; switching off the TV doesn't affect the fridge.

flashcards.definition: P=VI (W). Also P=I²R, P=V²/R. 1 W = 1 J/s.
flashcards.example: 12 V, 2 A → P=24 W. Transfers 24 J every second.

flashcards.definition: Energy unit: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 million J. Used for electricity billing.
flashcards.example: 2 kW heater for 3 h = 6 kWh. At £0.30/kWh = £1.80.

flashcards.definition: Safety device: thin wire melts if current exceeds rating → breaks circuit. Rated 3A, 5A, 13A.
flashcards.example: 13 A fuse in a 2300 W kettle (I=P/V=10 A) — would blow if current exceeds 13 A.

flashcards.definition: Green/yellow safety wire connecting metal case to ground. Prevents electric shock from fault.
flashcards.example: If live wire touches metal case, current flows to earth → fuse blows → power disconnected.

flashcards.definition: Buildup of charge on insulators by friction. Electrons transferred between surfaces.
flashcards.example: Rubbing balloon on hair → hair repels (all strands become like-charged).

flashcards.definition: DC: current flows one direction (batteries). AC: current alternates direction (mains — 50 Hz UK).
flashcards.example: Phone charger converts AC mains (230 V) to DC (5 V) for the battery.

questions.stem: R=10 Ω, I=3 A. Voltage?
questions.explanation: Using Ohm's Law: $V=IR=3\times10=30\text{ V}$.

questions.stem: Two identical lamps in series. Current through each:
choices: Same as total — series current is everywhere equal
questions.explanation: In series, current is the same at all points. Ammeter readings would be identical.

questions.stem: Why are homes wired in parallel?
choices: Each appliance gets full voltage, can be switched independently
questions.explanation: Parallel: 230 V to each appliance, independent switching, fault isolation.

questions.stem: 2000 W kettle used 0.5 h. Energy in kWh?
questions.explanation: 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh.

questions.stem: V=12 V, R=4 Ω. Current?
questions.explanation: Rearranging Ohm's Law: $I=V/R=12/4=3\text{ A}$.

questions.stem: Two 10 Ω resistors in parallel. Total resistance?
questions.explanation: 1/R=1/10+1/10=2/10. R=5 Ω. Parallel R < smallest individual R.

questions.stem: Ammeters are connected in ___ ; voltmeters in ___ .
questions.explanation: Ammeter: series (same current). Voltmeter: parallel (measures PD across component).

questions.stem: Why does a filament lamp's I-V graph curve?
choices: Resistance increases as filament heats up → current rises more slowly
Current is constant regardless of voltage
questions.explanation: As current flows, filament temperature rises. Metal ions vibrate more → more electron collisions → higher resistance → I-V curve flattens.

questions.stem: Hair stands up after removing a hat due to:
choices: Static electricity — friction transfers electrons, hairs become like-charged and repel
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons. Each hair gains same charge → mutual repulsion → hairs stand apart.

questions.stem: A 2300 W heater at 230 V. What fuse rating is appropriate?
choices: 13 A (I = P/V = 2300/230 = 10 A, next standard fuse up)
questions.explanation: I=2300/230=10 A → 13 A fuse (next standard rating above operating current).

questions.stem: Appliance is double-insulated. What does this mean for the earth wire?
choices: Not needed — plastic case cannot become live
questions.explanation: Double insulation (symbol: square within square) means the appliance has two layers of insulation. Plastic case → no earth needed.

questions.stem: Three 6 Ω resistors in series. Total R?
questions.explanation: R_total = 6+6+6 = 18 Ω. Series: add resistances.

questions.stem: Charge 30 C flows past a point in 5 s. Current?
questions.explanation: Current is charge over time: $I=Q/t=30/5=6\text{ A}$.

questions.stem: What does an RCD (Residual Current Device) do?
choices: Detects current leakage (live≠neutral) and cuts power in milliseconds, preventing electrocution
questions.explanation: RCDs detect imbalances as small as 30 mA between live and neutral. If current is leaking (e.g., through a person to earth), it trips — saving lives.

questions.stem: 0.5 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor for 60 s. Energy transferred?
A 500 W washing machine runs for 4 h. Energy used in kWh?
questions.explanation: Convert watts to kilowatts first: 500 W = 0.5 kW. Then $E=Pt=0.5\times4=2\text{ kWh}$. Using 500 directly gives the 2000 kWh trap.

questions.stem: A 6 Ω and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Total resistance?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{R}=\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $R=2\ \Omega$. The 9 Ω option is the series sum — adding is wrong for parallel. Parallel R is always less than the smallest branch.

questions.stem: To measure the voltage across a lamp, a voltmeter must be connected:
choices: Anywhere in the loop — position does not matter
questions.explanation: A voltmeter measures the potential difference BETWEEN two points, so it connects in parallel across the component. An ammeter would go in series instead.

questions.stem: Which description matches the I-V graph of a diode?
choices: Current flows easily in one direction but is almost zero in reverse
A straight line through the origin
A curve that flattens as the component heats up
Current is the same at every voltage
questions.explanation: A diode only conducts in one direction: large current when forward-biased, near-zero current in reverse. The straight line is an ohmic resistor; the flattening curve is a filament lamp.

questions.stem: A balloon rubbed on hair then sticks to a wall because:
choices: Friction charges the balloon; it induces opposite charge on the wall's surface and attraction holds it
The balloon becomes heavier than air
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons onto the balloon, giving it a static charge. The charged balloon attracts the neutral wall by inducing opposite charge on its surface — unlike charges attract.

questions.stem: A 920 W microwave runs on 230 V mains. Which fuse rating should be fitted?
questions.explanation: $I=\dfrac{P}{V}=\dfrac{920}{230}=4\text{ A}$. Choose the next standard rating above 4 A, so a 5 A fuse. A 3 A fuse would melt in normal use; 13 A is too high to protect properly.

questions.stem: A 4 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in series. Total resistance?
questions.explanation: In series, resistances add: $R=4+12=16\ \Omega$. The 3 Ω option is the parallel answer ($\dfrac{4\times12}{4+12}$) — a common mix-up.

questions.stem: A current of 2 A flows through a wire for 3 minutes. How much charge passes?
questions.explanation: Convert minutes to seconds first: 3 min = 180 s. Then $Q=It=2\times180=360\text{ C}$. Using 3 instead of 180 gives the 6 C trap.

questions.stem: A 12 V car headlamp draws 5 A for 10 minutes. Energy transferred?
questions.explanation: Convert 10 min to 600 s. $E=VIt=12\times5\times600=36000\text{ J}$. Using 10 instead of 600 s gives the 600 J trap; 60 J is just the power in watts.

questions.stem: What does the earth wire in a plug do?
choices: Carries current safely to the ground if a fault makes the metal case live, so the fuse blows
Completes the circuit during normal operation
Carries the alternating voltage to the appliance
questions.explanation: The earth wire (green/yellow) is a safety wire: if the live wire touches the metal case, current flows to ground, the large current blows the fuse and disconnects the supply. The neutral wire completes the circuit in normal use.
